scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Contact Improvisation was originated in 1972 by American dancer and choreographer Steve Paxton.

During a tour with the Grand Union collective at Oberlin College in January 1972, Paxton taught morning somatic sessions termed the 'Small Dance' alongside athletic afternoon rehearsals exploring disorientation, falls, rolls, and collisions.
This work produced 'Magnesium', a seminal performance on gym mats featuring young male students throwing their bodies into unbalance.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Emerging in the counter-cultural aftermath of the late 1960s, CI was conceived as an egalitarian, anti-spectacular practice echoing Yvonne Rainer's 'No Manifesto'.
Rejecting choreographic hierarchy, theatrical illusion, and gendered partnering roles, CI frames dance as real-time physical research and mutual listening.
It is practised globally in weekly community jams, multi-day residential festivals (such as the Breitenbush Jam and Earthdance gatherings), educational conservatories, and performance art venues.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The practice is built around an ongoing physical dialogue between two or more movers governed by gravity, momentum, friction, and shared weight.
Rather than counting beats or executing fixed choreographic phrases, dancers maintain continuous physical contact, listening kinesthetically through a rolling point of touch.
Watch for Small Dance, Aikido Roll, Table-Top.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Sources do not describe a specific musical tradition, meter, or prescribed musical accompaniment for Contact Improvisation.

Historically, early performances like 'Contact Improvisations' at the John Weber Gallery were presented alongside ambient gallery elements and a concurrent film screening (George Manupelli's Dr. Chicago).

Contact Improvisation has no set instrumentation, score, or tempo described in primary sources. Jams and stagings frequently unfold in complete acoustic silence punctuated only by audible breath, feet sliding on wood, clothes brushing against canvas or skin, and the dull thuds of body weight dropping onto sprung floors or mats.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Participants dance casually in comfortable, non-restrictive clothing such as sweatpants, tracksuits, leotards, or loose T-shirts chosen specifically to facilitate movement and friction while avoiding zippers or hard hardware.
CI takes place in open studios, residential dance centers, art galleries, bookstores, and theaters, usually on sprung wooden floors, gym mats, or tatami.
The physical environment is informal and non-hierarchical, designed for uninhibited rolling and floor work.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key originators and organizers include founder Steve Paxton; Nancy Stark Smith, who danced in the earliest performances, established the 'Contact Newsletter', co-edited 'Contact Quarterly', and developed the 'Underscore'; Lisa Nelson, pioneer of the 'Tuning Scores' and video documentation; Nita Little and Curt Siddall (early Oberlin and Bennington collaborators); Daniel Lepkoff; Mary Fulkerson; Barbara Dilley; and Nancy Topf.
Following its Manhattan debut, the practice dispersed through regional North American centers including New York, Boston, San Francisco, and Montreal.
Developed out of 1960s postmodern dance, the Judson Dance Theater, and the Grand Union collective.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Contact Improvisation is influence of Aikido: Steve Paxton drew directly upon aikido falling and rolling techniques to ensure safety during momentum-driven collisions.
Contact Improvisation is parent of Modern dance: Paxton developed the form following his professional training in the companies of Merce Cunningham and José Limón.
Contact Improvisation is parent of Judson Dance Theater: Rooted in the 1960s experimental collective where Paxton, Barbara Dilley, and Yvonne Rainer questioned the conventions of dance.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Relaxed, alert, and grounded with softened joints, ready to yield to gravity or absorb a partner's weight.
Used primarily as responsive sensors and structural supports rather than decorative gestures; grasping is minimized in favor of continuous rolling contact.
The primary fulcrum for weight exchange; rolling along the ribcage, pelvis, and back to share and redirect gravitational mass.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Small Dance: Stand upright in stillness, eyes open or soft, noticing micro-weight shifts and postural adjustments along the vertical axis.
Step 2: Aikido Roll: Soften knees, curve the spine diagonally, and roll smoothly across the floor across the diagonal of the back without striking bony prominences.
Footwork from the sources: Uncodified, shifting fluidly between barefoot floor contact, weight-bearing lunges, and suspended flight.
Drill: Stand in the Small Dance for 3 minutes, tracking micro-sways in the feet.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Table-Top Support: Drop to hands and knees with a stable spine, allowing a partner to drape or roll their torso across the back.
Step 4: Rolling Point of Contact: Make physical touch with a partner's arm, back, or shoulder; move together without sliding, rolling the contact point continuously across surfaces.
Drill: Practice aikido shoulder rolls along diagonal lines across the mat.

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Rest back-to-back with a partner, finding mutual equilibrium without moving feet.
